blueprint.summary: Connect named quantities and coordinates to vector geometry, matrix maps and tensor operations; predict both the shape and meaning of a calculation before using code.
outcomes: Name coordinate, axis and unit conventions
Compute and interpret vector sums, norms, dot products and projections
Explain a matrix through its column images and row weighted sums
Trace matrix products and composition order
Diagnose rank loss and basic solvability
Track tensor values through reductions, reindexing and broadcasting
sequence: Name quantities and shapes
Build vectors from coordinate directions
Connect dot products to projection
Apply matrix columns to transform geometry
Trace row-column products and affine batches
Reason about composition and lost information
Track named tensor axes and reductions
Diagnose shape-valid errors and practise independent transfer

visual.type: Coordinate projection, basis-image transformation, linked row-column contraction and tensor source-cell reduction
visual.question: Which quantities contribute to this output, and what relationship survives the operation?
visual.interaction: Change coordinates or a map, trace one product cell, and select a reduction axis to inspect its exact source values.

practice.task: Derive a projection, compare map order, compute a resource batch, repair broadcasting and reduce a measurement tensor without mixing examples.
practice.success: Correct hand values and shapes, interpreted units, perpendicular residual, explicit edge cases and a justified limit; independently verified runnable variations.

misconceptions: A vector dimension equals its number of array axes
A large dot product means similar direction regardless of length
Elementwise and matrix multiplication are interchangeable
Matching sizes establish semantic compatibility
Transpose and reshape do the same operation
Every matrix has an inverse
A legal broadcast is necessarily meaningful
blueprint.reviewFocus: Real/complex and row/column conventions; exact geometry, units, rank and source-cell provenance; NumPy broadcast/reindex semantics and floating-point caveats; independent numerical and browser evidence.

blueprint.summary: Use simpler matrix factors to solve equations, fit inconsistent observations, construct covariance and control low-rank approximation error.
outcomes: Trace elimination and solve PA=LU through two triangular systems
Construct perpendicular directions and justify a QR least-squares solution
Derive and validate a small Cholesky factor and its covariance interpretation
Follow SVD input/output directions and calculate rank-truncation error
Distinguish factor reconstruction, residual, numerical rank and conditioning
sequence: Read triangular, orthogonal and diagonal factors as operations
Eliminate equations, pivot and reuse LU factors
Remove shared column directions and project a noisy target
Construct correlated variation and diagnose covariance boundaries
Decompose independent stretches, approximate rank and inspect error
Diagnose numerical sensitivity and rank-deficient solutions
Solve independent calibration, covariance and rank-budget tasks

visual.type: linked factor operations with domain-specific geometric investigations
visual.question: What does each factor change, and which property makes the resulting task easier?
visual.interaction: Step pivoted equations; remove a projected column component; vary correlation; follow a vector through analytically constructed singular factors and truncate a direction.

practice.task: Fit a changed calibration dataset, repair row operations, construct a covariance factor and choose a rank from an error budget.
practice.success: Hand reasoning agrees with independent numeric checks; the learner states shape, assumptions, residual/error meaning and a changed-condition consequence.

misconceptions: An invertible matrix can have a zero first pivot before row reordering
A nonzero least-squares residual is not automatically an incorrect solve
A valid covariance can be semidefinite and fail ordinary Cholesky
A successful Cholesky call does not itself check both triangles for symmetry
SVD factors can change signs or tied bases without changing the matrix
Low rank does not automatically mean storage savings or removal of noise
Small residuals do not prove insensitive or accurately estimated parameters
blueprint.reviewFocus: Full individual design and claim ledger: docs/teaching/MATRIX-DECOMPOSITIONS-LESSON-DESIGN.md. Keep the local eigenvalue bridge because the recorded prerequisite is later in module order. Review shape/permutation conventions, numerical versus exact rank, original example outputs, meaningful visuals, and production isolation.

blueprint.summary: Find directions preserved by a square map, use a valid eigenbasis to separate changes, and interpret spectra in repeated updates, data variation and physical modes.
outcomes: Derive and verify a small eigenpair through a shifted null space
Distinguish signed scales, zero output, repeated eigenspaces and a defective basis
Use diagonalization with its correct inverse and identify symmetric structure
Separate eventual decay, finite transient growth and initial-mode participation
Derive a variance-maximizing direction and its reconstruction error
Choose an appropriate numerical routine and interpret residuals, gaps and failed iteration starts
sequence: Preserve a line under a transformation
Derive a characteristic equation and its null spaces
Change to an eigenbasis and examine exceptions
Trace repeated updates and stability boundaries
Measure and retain variance along a direction
Interpret mixing, graph smoothing and coupled vibration modes
Compute, verify and diagnose an eigenpair
Solve independent changed-matrix and interpretation tasks

visual.type: Equal-scale direction geometry, raw recurrence trajectories and projected point clouds
visual.question: Which part of a change stays along a direction, and what does its signed scale mean in this model?
visual.interaction: Turn a unit input across six maps; compare six repeated-update rules and three initial vectors; project three small datasets while calculating variance and squared error.

practice.task: Find a changed spectrum and rank-one approximation; repair a stability claim; construct a new mixing rule; interpret a tied covariance variance budget.
practice.success: Correct original-coordinate checks, explicit assumptions and units, consistent variance/error denominators, and explanations of what numerical and application results do not establish.

misconceptions: Zero is an eigenvector because it satisfies the equation
Negative scales or zero outputs cannot be eigenvalues
Every square matrix has a real eigenbasis
Repeated eigenvalues always prevent diagonalization
The inverse of any eigenvector matrix is its transpose
Eigenvalues inside the unit disk guarantee decreasing norm at every step
A small residual certifies the dominant eigenpair
Leading covariance directions are necessarily meaningful signal
Discrete and continuous dynamics share the same decay test
blueprint.reviewFocus: Keep the nonzero definition, eigenvalue/vector pairing, field and multiplicity distinctions, quantitative variance fixture, stability exceptions and numerical-contract boundaries. Derived visuals must match the independently checked model and use equal geometric scales. Preserve module position and actual next Jacobian topic.

blueprint.summary: Explain a derivative as a local linear map, propagate sensitivities through vector and matrix computations, and derive and independently check a complete affine backward pass.
outcomes: Interpret Jacobian entries, units, shape and evaluation point
Separate a directional rate, predicted change and actual output
Apply the chain rule in order and distinguish JVP from VJP
Derive matrix-shaped weight, bias and input gradients
Diagnose finite-difference errors, kinks and loss scaling
Connect matrix operators to solves, normalized outputs and curvature
sequence: Refresh scalar slopes and product rules
Construct a Jacobian one partial at a time
Compare exact and local changes
Compose local maps
Pull back scalar gradients and sum shared paths
Derive affine batch gradients entrywise
Run and check a complete objective
Compute derivative products with automatic differentiation
Explore matrix operators and independent transfer

visual.type: Linked nonlinear/tangent curves, directed forward/reverse traces, parameter contribution matrices and computed finite-difference errors
visual.question: Which local input changes or sensitivity contributions determine this result?
visual.interaction: Change the base point and direction, propagate derivative stages, select a shared parameter and compare objective reductions or numerical step sizes.

practice.task: Calculate and interpret a changed Jacobian, reverse a new scalar objective, repair a batch reduction error and design independent derivative checks.
practice.success: Correct rates and shapes, explicit row/column and averaging conventions, explained path sums, valid finite-difference controls and recognition of smoothness/rounding limits.

misconceptions: A Jacobian returns the new output rather than its local change
Every existing partial derivative establishes differentiability
Reverse gradients invert the forward values
Matching shapes prove the chain order is correct
Shared bias gradients should always be averaged
AD is finite differences or exact real arithmetic
Smaller finite-difference steps always improve accuracy
A returned derivative at a kink proves differentiability
blueprint.reviewFocus: Differentiability versus partials; Euclidean/Frobenius row/column conventions; output versus parameter axes; objective reduction; independent complex-step and finite-difference assumptions; source-specific autodiff APIs and numerical limitations.

blueprint.summary: Read tensor computations as named-axis products and reductions, verify their meaning, and distinguish array operations from coordinate-independent tensor structure.
outcomes: Translate a complete sum into explicit einsum and predict shape and entries
Distinguish diagonal selection, reduction, batching, broadcasting and output permutation
Implement and check covariance and masked scaled dot-product attention
Compare contraction orders using operation counts and temporary shapes
Preserve vector, linear-functional and metric meaning under a stated basis change
sequence: Name axes and fix one output entry
Expose product terms and reduced indices
Separate diagonal selection from summation
Track batches and broadcast groups
Compute centered covariance and attention
Choose an execution order
Separate components from geometric objects
Diagnose numerical and shape-valid mistakes
Practise independent transfer

visual.type: Selectable contraction terms, query-to-key contribution rows, two contraction trees and a linked basis/coordinate diagram
visual.question: Which input entries determine this output, and what changes when labels, execution order or basis change?
visual.interaction: Edit a bounded explicit expression, inspect a selected output, change attention masks, compare matrix dimensions, and change the coordinate basis while checking invariant quantities.

practice.task: Derive new contractions, repair an accidental cross-batch result, compute centered covariance, choose an order and preserve a measurement in a new basis.
practice.success: Correct entries and axes, explanatory index ranges, independent loop/library agreement, explicit centering and normalization, and preservation of coordinate-independent values.

misconceptions: Every repeated label is summed
A repeated label inside one operand means an ordinary product
Equal axis sizes imply equal meaning
A shared batch label must disappear
Einsum performs softmax or centering
A lower multiplication count is a measured speedup
An arbitrary ndarray determines a mathematical tensor transformation law
blueprint.reviewFocus: Explicit versus implicit conventions, diagonal dimension requirements, singleton and ellipsis broadcasting, dtype/view/conjugation behavior, masking, covariance denominator, cost-model limits and vector/covector/metric basis transformations.

blueprint.summary: Use random matrix products to discover a low-rank space, compress a least-squares problem or estimate an operator trace, while preserving the correct error and probability contracts.
